A1.justification: Both readable 13-page PDFs describe DoDo-Code, with matching core methods and experiments despite substantial revision. All pages, equations, figures and tables support comparison. Neither PDF contains an appendix.

before.justification: Sections 2.1–2.3 report original codebook construction, segment-correction and timing experiments, plus simulated long-sequence decoding and outer Reed–Solomon results.

after.justification: Sections 5.1–5.4 report original embedding visualizations, codebook and loss-ablation results, segment-correction failures and timings. Retained experiments also qualify as original empirical results.

M1.justification: V2 removes the DFS-based long-sequence decoder and outer Reed–Solomon construction described in v1 Sections 2.3 and 3.4, substantially reducing the proposed system's functionality. The CNN embedding, truncated-loss formulation, density-guided codeword selection and K-d-tree segment correction remain.

E1.justification: V2 retains synthetic short 4-ary code experiments but removes evaluation of approximately 150-nucleotide concatenated sequences with multiple IDS errors and outer coding. Section 5.1 adds an illustrative binary length-10 code experiment, introducing a different alphabet population.

E2.justification: V2 adds the original-PNLL variant DEGS* to Table 1 and evaluates a VT code in the new binary visualization. Rand remains, as do the Cai et al. and Gabrys et al. code-rate comparators and the brute-force timing baseline.

E3.justification: Table 2 changes from 100,000 to 100 million single-edit trials and adds k=5 reporting; Figure 5 timing still uses 100,000 segments. New protocols include an original-PNLL control and an eight-dimensional binary embedding projected using t-SNE. The long-sequence protocol, including 1% equiprobable IDS corruption and SeqER/SegER metrics, disappears.

E4.justification: V2 adds a controlled original-versus-revised PNLL ablation and embedding-space case studies comparing greedy search, random search and VT codewords. It removes v1's restricted-multiple-error diagnostic, failed-segment analysis and outer-RS redundancy sweep. The existing greedy-versus-random comparison and neighbor-count sensitivity analysis remain.

E5.justification: Both versions report codebook means and maxima over 10 runs. V2 adds ± values to Table 1 without defining the statistic they represent. V1's Figure 7 reporting means and standard deviations over five RS experiments is removed.

E6.justification: V2 adds DEGS* results, including 35,720.4 mean codewords at n=11, and binary visualization findings. Table 2 supplies replacement counts under the much larger sample and adds k=5; zero k=4 failures persist. Long-sequence and RS results disappear. Existing Rand/DEGS cardinalities, the 68.9% code rate and Figure 5 timing values are unchanged.

T1.justification: V2 adds the O(m|C(n)|) tree-memory bound and explicit CNN inference and cost assumptions, while removing DFS complexity estimates. Both already distinguish O(n) single-neighbor decoding from O(n²) decoding with Levenshtein rechecks. The redundancy argument remains unproved; v1's numbered conjecture becomes informal speculation.

C1.justification: V2 narrows the main contribution to short single-IDS-correcting codebooks and segment decoding. It removes the long-sequence/RS solution and its claimed 67.5% combined rate. Claims of superior short-code rates, apparent optimality and being the first deep-learning-designed IDS code remain.

C2.justification: V2 adds interpretations of the binary visualization, particularly that uncovered sequences suggest opportunities to enlarge VT codebooks. It removes v1's substantive conclusions about multiple errors causing long-sequence failures, recovery of segment boundaries after failures and mitigation through outer RS coding. The lack of an optimality proof remains acknowledged.

D1.justification: V2 explicitly specifies the PNLL base loss, discloses the default 64-dimensional embedding, supplies Algorithm 1 and discusses deterministic codebook regeneration. The repository changes from promised future availability to stated availability. V1's long-decoder and RS finite-field implementation details are removed; the PDFs do not establish a changed default embedding configuration.

R1.justification: V2 adds a dedicated discussion distinguishing DoDo-Code from neural channel codes such as ProductAE and CrossMPT through IDS handling and explicit codebooks. It expands burst-error, segmented-code and recent codebook-generation references while removing substantial DNA-pipeline, DFS and RS background, materially revising research positioning.

P1.justification: The title, abstract and introduction are extensively rewritten. V2 separates related work and BDD background, places methods before experiments, expands the loss explanation and adds a Conclusion and Limitations section. This substantially changes the narrative beyond inserting new experiments.

P2.justification: V2 adopts a NeurIPS layout with resized and wrapped figures. The greedy-search flowchart is replaced by Algorithm 1, the Siamese diagram moves from Figure 8 to Figure 1, and a binary visualization is added. DFS/long-sequence/RS displays and Table 3 disappear; Tables 1 and 2 gain rows.

improvement.justification: V2 better supports the retained short-code contribution through the PNLL control and zero k=4 failures across 100 million rather than 100,000 trials. Explicit loss specification, pseudocode and model/access documentation also improve reproducibility. Removing DFS/RS experiments sacrifices end-to-end DNA-storage validation, but accompanies narrower application claims. The net gain is modest: optimality remains unproved and the new ± statistics are undefined.
